analysis.one_liner: Requires corporations to get majority shareholder approval before spending on political campaigns.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors after its sponsor referred it to the House Administration Committee in February 2010; it never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced a month after the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision allowed corporations to spend general treasury money on political ads, this bill would have required a corporation to win a vote of majority approval from its own shareholders at an annual meeting before paying for any independent political expenditure or electioneering ad. Company officers and directors would have been personally liable for a penalty equal to any spending made without that approval, with small exceptions for minor spending. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders of public corporations — including ordinary workers whose pensions and 401(k)s hold company stock — would gain control over whether corporate money they partly own is spent on politics. Voters generally would benefit from a requirement that corporate political spending face a check from the people whose money it is, and corporate officers would gain clarity about their legal exposure.

how_it_helps.text: Would require that a majority of shareholders approve, at an annual meeting, before a corporation can spend general treasury money on independent political expenditures or electioneering communications, giving the owners of the money a say in how it is used politically.

Would make each corporate officer and director personally liable for a civil penalty equal to the amount of any political spending made without shareholder approval, adding real consequences rather than a fine absorbed by the company.

Would spare small corporations from the requirement for minor political spending — under $8,000 a year for companies with fewer than 100 full-time employees, under $20,000 for others — so the rule targets large-scale corporate election spending.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that want to spend treasury money on politics would bear the cost of annual shareholder votes and the risk of penalties; their officers and directors would be personally on the hook for any illegal spending. Companies would also face added administrative burden of putting political-spending proposals to shareholder votes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations and their officers and directors

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly leaves corporate PACs (separate segregated funds) untouched, so a major established channel of corporate political money — funded through voluntary employee contributions and run under existing disclosure rules — would continue exactly as before.

Requiring a majority of ALL shareholders to vote approval is a very high bar, since annual-meeting turnout is typically far below half of outstanding shares. In practice most corporations would be unable to clear it, making the provision function closer to a ban on treasury-funded political ads than a genuine consent mechanism.
The dollar thresholds carve out smaller political spending entirely, so a corporation could spend $7,999 a year on election ads (or $19,999 if larger) with no shareholder vote at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real problem opened by Citizens United — corporate managers spending treasury money on politics without approval from the shareholders who own it — and the personal-liability penalty gives it teeth. But the design is uneven: the corporate PAC carve-out leaves a big existing spending channel alone, and the majority-of-all-shareholders standard is so hard to meet that the requirement operates more as a near-prohibition than a workable consent process. As a first step to reassert shareholder control it was directionally reasonable; as drafted it was a blunt instrument that likely would have drawn constitutional and practical challenges.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Sestak introduced the bill on February 22, 2010, roughly a month after the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision allowed corporations to spend treasury money on election ads.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day and received no hearing, no markup, and no further action of any kind for the rest of the Congress.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with no committee or floor support behind it.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired in committee without ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations and their executives are better off: the Citizens United ruling stands unmodified by Congress, so companies can still spend general treasury money on independent political advertising without asking shareholders, and corporate PACs continue untouched. The absence of any cosponsors or committee action means the proposal never became a serious legislative threat to that status quo.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their political spending programs
industries.note: The bill would have required shareholder approval before corporate treasury money could fund independent political ads, and imposed personal penalties on officers and directors for spending without it. Industry interest runs against the public here because unapproved corporate political spending amplifies corporate voice in elections using money that partly belongs to ordinary retirement savers.

industries.industry: Corporate political action committees (separate segregated funds)
industries.note: The bill expressly exempts corporate PACs from the shareholder-approval requirement, locking in the existing corporate PAC channel as the unaffected route for corporate-linked political money. PAC money comes from voluntary employee contributions rather than the corporate treasury, so its interest does not sit squarely against the public's, but the carve-out preserved that channel untouched.
